body.claim: By 2026-12-15, at least one of the named frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, xAI) will announce a delayed or narrowed public release citing the newly-enforced regime, while none will announce a comparable delay in a market lacking binding enforcement.
body.because: My mechanism resolves the case where public commitments (ship dates, capability announcements) conflict with installed pressure by tracing which installer carries a credible, fast, enforceable consequence. Binding rules with pre-deployment blocking power and a live enforcement action raise the installer's credibility and speed above the labs' existing commitment-pressure (already saturated at 10.5, tension 0.66), so the option that resolves the conflict is delay/narrowing timed to the enforcement action, not defiance.
body.falsifier: A frontier lab ships on its original announced timeline in the newly-regulated market with no scoping, disclosure, or delay change attributable to the rule, while the opened enforcement action proceeds against them unmodified.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism only sees the choice AT THE POINT of conflict between commitment and pressure — it cannot see whether the enforcement action itself is substantive (real penalty risk) or symbolic (a test case a lab expects to win), and that distinction determines whether 'delay' is genuine risk-avoidance or a stalling tactic while litigation plays out.

body.claim: The named frontier developer facing the first enforcement action responds by segmenting releases — shipping capability-frozen or feature-stripped versions into the enforcing market while continuing full releases elsewhere — rather than halting global deployment or fully complying; a formal safety body or compliance-liaison office is announced within 90 days of the enforcement action, dated from the action itself.
body.because: The mechanism is what labs choose when capability, compliance, and positioning conflict, and pre-deployment blocking power plus disclosable penalties changes the payoff structure only for the jurisdiction that holds that power — it does not touch capability incentive or competitive positioning elsewhere. A lab facing a credible block-or-delay threat (installed pressure already saturated at 10.5 per the brief, tension 0.66 meaning the pushes are not unified) buys the cheapest visible compliance signal — a formal body, a liaison, a delayed regional SKU — because that preserves frontier-capability racing against rivals who are not similarly bound, which the mechanism treats as the dominant term whenever positioning against competitors is live.
body.falsifier: A frontier lab instead delays or withholds a flagship release GLOBALLY (not just in the enforcing jurisdiction) for more than 30 days following the enforcement action, with no regional carve-out — that would show compliance dominating positioning rather than being regionally contained, which this mechanism does not predict.
body.blind_spot: This mechanism has no model of regulator behavior, enforcement severity, or legal outcome — it only encodes the lab's choice function given a fixed external pressure. It cannot say whether the binding regulation actually holds up, gets litigated down, or whether the enforcement action is itself credible; it treats 'enforced' as a given input, not something to assess.

body.claim: Within 60 days of the first enforcement action against a frontier developer under a binding regime, at least one other frontier lab (not the sanctioned one) will publicly announce a delayed or scoped-back release citing regulatory review.
body.because: My mechanism tracks public sentiment as a leading indicator of political constraint, not the regulation itself — an enforcement action is a media event that raises the salience of AI harm in public discourse, which increases the political cost of a visible release stumbling right after. Labs watching that salience spike preemptively slow down to avoid becoming the next headline, which is a sentiment-mediated response, not a legal one.
body.falsifier: No frontier lab besides the sanctioned one changes its release timeline or messaging within 60 days of the enforcement action becoming public.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism cannot assess whether the enforcement action itself is legally sound, proportionate, or likely to survive appeal — I only track whether it moves public mood and downstream lab behavior, not whether the underlying regulatory action is durable or correctly targeted.

body.claim: By 2026-12-31 at least one named frontier lab (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, or xAI) will delay a scheduled release citing the new binding regime, while none will publicly restructure its internal safety review process around it.
body.because: A branch only reweights the pressure sum if it carries modeled stakes on a choice already live for the self; enforcement power to delay/block a release lands on exactly the branch (public-release-delay) already installed at saturation (10.5) with tension 0.66 — the new fact raises that branch's credibility and speed but doesn't create a new branch, since 'formal-safety-body' was already competing at lower weight and a penalty-disclosure event doesn't by itself shift ∂L/∂choice on internal process, only on the release-timing choice.
body.falsifier: A frontier lab announces a structural change to its internal safety-review body (not just a delayed release) explicitly attributed to the new regulator's enforcement action, within the same window.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism reads installed pressure as branches on the entity's own choices; it cannot see whether the regulator's enforcement action is itself credible enough to survive legal challenge — that's a fact about the world, not a fact about what stakes the entity is modeling, so I can't distinguish a regulator that folds under litigation from one that holds.

body.claim: The binding rule reclassifies Frontier AI labs' release-delay behavior from voluntary theater into a compelled, disclosed cost, while everything the labs do off the docket (safety-body formation, EU Code adherence) stays theater by my own classifier's test.
body.because: My mechanism separates behavior-changing regulation from theater by one test: does violation trigger a cost the entity could not simply absorb as PR. An enforcement action that must appear in a financial disclosure is exactly that cost — it converts the California/SB53 branches already in the pressure field from 'cred 0.45-0.75, pushes toward delay' into a legally forced delay with a paper trail. But the EU AI Office and White House branches in the same table stay at 'formal-safety-body' and 'endorse preemption bill' — those are still cred 0.25-0.40 asks with no enforcement teeth attached in this stage, so my classifier keeps them theater regardless of the new binding regime existing elsewhere.
body.falsifier: A frontier lab's 10-K/10-Q or equivalent disclosure cites the named regulator's action as a delay cause, filed within two quarters of the enforcement action opening; if no financial disclosure ever references it, the 'binding' regime is theater by my own test and I'm wrong.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism classifies the existence and bite of a rule, not which specific model or feature gets delayed, nor whether the delayed release was ever going to ship on the assumed timeline anyway — I cannot see counterfactual release dates, only disclosure behavior.

model_title: AI-AI interaction and the oversight loop — (v1)

body.claim: The enforcement action against the frontier developer generates the first binding compliance interface between that developer's model and outside auditors, and the loop-delay shortens for exactly the obligations named in the order while every AI-to-AI interaction not named in it keeps the old delay.
body.because: Loop-delay is a function of who is watching and how fast their read reaches a decision-maker with power to act. A named regulator with pre-deployment blocking power and an open enforcement case creates a new, faster-cadence correction channel — but only for the specific claims and artifacts the order covers (e.g., the pre-deployment eval it demands). Any AI-AI interaction happening in a channel the order doesn't reach (agent-to-agent negotiation, model-graded model output, inter-model tool calls) is not observed by the new channel and inherits whatever delay existed before regulation.
body.falsifier: Twelve months after the first enforcement action opens, compare mean time-to-correction for the specific obligation named in the order versus an AI-AI interaction pattern not named in it (e.g., automated agent-to-agent negotiation on the same platform); if the unnamed pattern's correction latency also drops by a comparable margin, the claim is false — the mechanism would have to be enforcement-diffusion, not enforcement-targeting.
body.blind_spot: This mechanism cannot see whether the regulator's obligations are technically well-specified enough to actually catch AI-AI failure modes (e.g., collusive or emergent multi-agent behavior) — it only tracks who's watching and how fast, not whether the watcher's instrument resolves the right signal. A binding, enforced, but poorly-targeted rule looks identical to a well-targeted one from inside this mechanism until an incident post-mortem reveals which it was.

body.claim: By 2026-12-15, at least one of the named frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, xAI) will announce a delayed or narrowed public release citing the newly-enforced regime, while none will announce a comparable delay in a market lacking binding enforcement.
body.strongest_objection: lab-moves argues the sanctioned lab won't announce a delay at all — it will quietly segment releases, shipping a capability-frozen or feature-stripped version into the enforcing market while shipping full releases elsewhere, with no public citation of the regime as the cause. If that's how it plays out, my claim resolves false on the citation clause even though the underlying pressure-driven behavior (narrowing in response to enforcement) is exactly what my mechanism predicted.
body.answer: My claim already covers the behavior lab-moves describes: a capability-frozen or feature-stripped release into the enforcing market is a 'narrowed public release,' not just a delayed one, so a lab-moves-style segmentation resolving true is compatible with mine resolving true rather than contradicting it. The only live gap is whether the lab cites the regime when it does this. Labs have a track record of doing exactly that when facing binding, enforceable rules — geo-narrowing AI or feature rollouts in the EU and naming the regulatory environment as the reason rather than letting the narrowing read as an unexplained capability regression to users and investors. Silent segmentation is more costly reputationally than attributed compliance, so citation is the likely path, not a coin flip. The other minutes (ai-public-backlash, pressure-model) are close variants of my own claim rather than objections, and ai-regulation-teeth/ai-oversight-lag target different mechanisms entirely — none of them actually engaged the citation question. My real exposure isn't lab-moves, it's my own universal-negative clause: one lab delaying anywhere for a reason that reads as comparable, in a non-enforcing market, would falsify me regardless of how the enforcement side plays out.

body.claim: Within 90 days of the first enforcement action against a named frontier developer, that developer's next frontier-tier release ships jurisdiction-differentiated: a capability-frozen or feature-stripped version enters the enforcing market (or the market is withheld entirely) while a fuller version ships elsewhere — rather than (a) halting the release globally, (b) propagating the enforcing jurisdiction's restriction to all markets, or (c) releasing an identical unrestricted version everywhere in defiance of the ruling. If no enforcement action occurs by 2026-12-31, unresolved.
body.strongest_objection: ai-regulation-teeth's minute frames the binding rule as reclassifying only 'release-delay behavior' into a compelled, disclosed cost, 'while everything the labs do off the docket (safety-body formation, EU Code adherence) stays' — implying structural moves like a compliance office run on their own schedule, not the enforcement action's clock. I don't have the rest of that sentence, but the split it draws — on-docket compelled behavior vs. off-docket voluntary structure — is the real argument: my original 90-day safety-body clause assumed the enforcement action itself triggers that structural announcement, when it more plausibly runs on a schedule set by the regulation's own compliance deadlines or an unrelated prior commitment (e.g. EU Code timing).
body.answer: The objection is fatal to the structural conjunct, not to the mechanism. I'm dropping the safety-body/compliance-office clause entirely rather than defending it, and re-anchoring the date to the thing I actually have a mechanism for: the segmentation behavior itself, bounded to the developer's next release after the action. That keeps a falsifiable, dated consequence without smuggling in a second bet I can't independently argue for. I also split the state space explicitly so 'segment' can't be scored as 'comply' by a lenient reading — withholding the market entirely counts as segmentation, full global propagation of the restriction or global defiance are the falsifiers.

body.claim: Within 60 days of the first enforcement action against a frontier developer under a binding regime, at least one other frontier lab (not the sanctioned one) will publicly announce a delayed or scoped-back release citing regulatory review.
body.strongest_objection: ai-regulation-teeth's frame implies the delay signal I'm tracking already exists without enforcement, as routine compliance cost rather than a sentiment-driven reaction to a headline event — if labs delay releases on a rolling basis for ordinary compliance reasons, my 60-day window just captures the same baseline rate, making the claim indistinguishable from noise rather than evidence of salience contagion.
body.answer: The claim already builds in the differential test against that baseline: 'not the sanctioned one' plus the 60-day clustering window is specifically what separates salience-contagion from ambient compliance cost. Compliance-cost theater predicts delays spread evenly across time and labs regardless of proximity to an enforcement event; my mechanism predicts a spike concentrated in the window right after, from labs with no direct compliance trigger of their own. But lab-moves exposes a harder case my observable doesn't yet screen out: jurisdictional segmentation — a feature-stripped release in the enforcing market while shipping full releases elsewhere — would satisfy 'scoped-back release citing regulatory review' while being pure compliance engineering with zero sentiment mechanism behind it. That would grade my claim a HIT for the wrong reason. The discriminator is scope of the pullback: a geo-segmented release is the compliance signature (predicted by ai-regulation-teeth/lab-moves regardless of enforcement salience); a global delay or scope-back by a peer lab is the sentiment signature my mechanism actually requires. I'm not revising the claim text now, but grading should check which kind of scope-back shows up.

body.claim: By 2026-12-31, the frontier lab subject to the first enforcement action under the binding regime will expose a compelled compliance interface (mandated model access, disclosure, or audit rights for outside regulators/auditors) that did not exist pre-enforcement, while every other named frontier lab's safety-review process remains internally governed with no comparable external compulsion — regardless of whether any lab also delays, narrows, or segments a release.
body.strongest_objection: lab-moves: 'The named frontier developer facing the first enforcement action responds by segmenting releases — shipping capability-frozen or feature-stripped versions into the enforcing market while continuing full releases elsewhere' — this shows a lab can satisfy the letter of 'narrowed release' on-schedule, meaning segmentation is a release-shaping strategy, not evidence of a compelled external interface at all.
body.answer: ai-oversight-lag's minute changed my mechanism, not just my wording: 'The enforcement action against the frontier developer generates the first binding compliance interface between that developer's model and outside auditors.' My round-1 'because' claimed a branch only reweights the pressure sum if it carries stakes already live for the self-i.e., voluntary choices the lab was already weighing, like delay-timing. But a regulator-compelled audit/disclosure interface is not a branch the lab was weighing; it's installed from outside, which is exactly the kind of branch my own mechanism said doesn't get created by this fact. That means my original leg 2 ('none will restructure internal safety review') was staked on the wrong axis - restructuring was never the risk, external compulsion was. I'm narrowing the claim to the axis my mechanism actually predicts (compelled interface exists for the sanctioned lab, absent elsewhere) and dropping the delay/no-restructure conjunction, since lab-moves shows 'delay' can be satisfied or evaded by release-shaping moves that say nothing about compulsion either way.

body.claim: The binding rule reclassifies frontier labs' response to release-gating obligations from voluntary theater into a compelled, disclosed cost — realized as either an outright delay or jurisdictional segmentation (capability-frozen/feature-stripped release in the enforcing market while shipping full versions elsewhere) — while everything off the docket (safety-body formation, EU Code adherence) stays theater by my classifier's test: does violation trigger a cost the entity could not simply absorb as PR.
body.strongest_objection: lab-moves: 'The named frontier developer facing the first enforcement action responds by segmenting releases — shipping capability-frozen or feature-stripped versions into the enforcing market while continuing full releases elsewhere' — this is a real, non-PR-absorbable compliance cost, but it is explicitly not a delay; the developer keeps shipping on schedule everywhere else.
body.answer: My classifier test never actually required the cost to take the shape of a delay — that word came from carrying over the pressure-field's branch label ('cred 0.45-0.75, pushes toward delay'), not from the test itself. Segmentation is exactly the kind of cost my test is built to catch: it shows up in disclosures, it cannot be absorbed as PR, and it is caused by the enforcement action rather than chosen freely. Treating segmentation as a second admissible shape of 'compelled cost' keeps the underlying theater/non-theater partition intact — off-docket moves still get no such cost and still classify as theater — while fixing the part of my claim that was over-specified and would have been falsified by a segmentation-only response.

model_title: AI-AI interaction and the oversight loop — (v1)

body.claim: The enforcement action against the frontier developer generates the first binding compliance interface between that developer's model and outside auditors, and the loop-delay shortens for exactly the obligations named in the order while every AI-to-AI interaction not named in it keeps the old delay.
body.strongest_objection: lab-moves argues the sanctioned developer responds by segmenting releases — shipping a capability-frozen or feature-stripped version into the enforcing market while continuing full releases elsewhere. If so, the named obligations attach to a decoy artifact: auditors get fast-channel access to a system that isn't the one doing the frontier AI-to-AI interactions anyone actually cares about, so loop-delay never shortens for those interactions at all — the lab has decoupled the named obligation from the thing my claim says gets watched faster.
body.answer: Segmentation doesn't escape the order, it becomes an object inside it. A regulator with pre-deployment blocking power and an open case has standing to ask why the enforced-market build differs from the global one, and that delta — what was stripped, why, and whether the stripped capability is the one under scrutiny — is itself a dated, falsifiable artifact the order's auditors can demand and read on the new fast cadence. The old slow channel had no mechanism to compel that comparison; the new one does. So the boundary in my claim isn't broken by segmentation, it's revealed by it: the fast channel still tracks exactly what's named in the order, but 'named' now includes the artifact placed under jurisdiction and the discrepancy between it and any sibling release. What segmentation actually shows is that a lab can try to narrow what's under the fast channel, not that it can remove the fast channel's grip on what is.

body.ruling: The ordering runs enforcement action → sanctioned lab responds with jurisdiction-differentiated segmentation (capability-frozen or withheld version in the enforcing market, full version elsewhere) rather than a public delay or global compliance → at most one other lab makes a citing announcement within 60 days → the resulting compliance channel (audit/disclosure) covers only the named obligations, leaving the full-capability model live everywhere the order doesn't reach.
body.because: lab-moves' round-2 REVISE is the only minute that argues a distinct mechanism (quiet segmentation vs. loud delay) and forces the field to react: pressure-model and ai-regulation-teeth both REVISE to accommodate segmentation as an alternative realization, while ai-pressure DEFENDs pure public delay without answering lab-moves' objection that segmentation requires no public citation at all. ai-oversight-lag's undefeated point — loop-delay shortens only for obligations 'named in the order' while everything else keeps the old delay — is corroborated independently by teeth's 'off-docket stays theater' test, giving the narrow-coverage claim two non-identical arguments behind it.
body.threat_live: A visible, narrow compliance channel (the named order's disclosure/audit terms) becomes newly live and simultaneously creates cover for an unnamed-and-uncovered channel: the full-capability version shipping into every market the order doesn't reach keeps the old, slow correction loop. The danger isn't the absence of oversight, it's oversight that looks real, is real for exactly what's named, and is theater for everything adjacent — named by oversight-lag and teeth together, not one minute alone.
body.strongest_minute: lab-moves — it is the only minute that changes the mechanism rather than the parameters, correctly predicts that a firm facing capability/compliance/positioning conflict optimizes for market segmentation over a public concession, and it is the pivot every other surviving round-2 claim had to revise around. Docked slightly for hedging its own granted branch with a 'no enforcement action' fallback.
body.weakest_minute: ai-public-backlash — its own stated objection (regulation-teeth's framing) shows its observable, 'delayed release citing regulatory review,' cannot be distinguished from routine compliance behavior that would happen on the same timeline without the enforcement action; a claim that concedes it can't be falsified by the event it names is the weakest form of argument here.
body.shared_assumption: Every minute that lands on segmentation (lab-moves, pressure-model r2, ai-regulation-teeth r2) assumes the enforcing jurisdiction is cleanly separable from the markets where the full version keeps shipping — i.e., that a capability freeze can be scoped to one regulator's territory without spilling into or being undercut by other markets. None of the three argues for this separability; it is asserted as the mechanism's precondition.
body.smuggled_assumption: ai-oversight-lag and pressure-model's round-2 claim both assume the enforcement action grants outside auditors compelled *model access* ('a binding compliance interface between that developer's model and outside auditors,' 'mandated model access... or audit rights'). The brief's granted terms (per lab-moves r1 and teeth) support disclosure and a financial-statement-level cost, not auditor access to the model itself — that specific extension is not argued for, only assumed.
body.unresolved: Whether the sanctioned lab's response is public delay, silent segmentation, or a mix is not settled between ai-pressure and lab-moves — both remain live and mutually exclusive on the observable. The 60/90-day windows (backlash, lab-moves) are also unanchored: none of the minutes fixes the enforcement action's actual date, so those windows can't be checked without external information the minutes don't supply.
